proposed.author: EditorDavid
proposed.description: "When we need medical care, we expect decisions about our treatment to be made by our doctors, not a tech company's algorithm," writes the EFF newsletter EFFector. But in January America's federal government launched a program called WISeR that uses AI to evaluate authorization requests for certain procedures from America's federal health insurance program for seniors, Medicare. EFF sued for records and discovered "additional issues" with the program that they say "could jeopardize Medicare beneficiaries' access to care." The records we received revealed that WISeR has resulted in widespread delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Further documents obtained by EFF show a rushed and rocky rollout, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments treat AI like a silver bullet for complex problems. EFF has now published hundreds of pages of documents obtained through our lawsuit, available here... The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. EFF has long argued that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples' rights or access to benefits, such as immigration enforcement and policing decisions. That's because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people's rights or deprive them of benefits they're entitle
proposed.title: EFF Criticizes US Government's Use of AI For Evaluating Senior Health Insurance Requests

proposed.author: World Eye
proposed.description: Open any live flight tracker and you'll see ten thousand aircraft moving smoothly across a map, each labelled with a callsign, altitude, speed and destination. It looks like the planes are reporting to the website. In a sense they are — but not to the website, and not over the internet. Every one of those dots is an aircraft continuously shouting its own position into the sky on a radio frequency, and anyone with a ~$30 receiver can hear it. That system is called ADS-B, and understanding it explains almost everything about how flight tracking works: why coverage is brilliant over Europe and patchy over oceans, why some aircraft vanish, and what you actually have to build if you want to render that firehose on a globe. I run WorldEye , where live flights are one layer on a real-time globe next to cameras, satellites and weather — this is the mental model I wish I'd had before wiring that layer up. ADS-B: the aircraft does the broadcasting ADS-B stands for Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast : Automatic — it transmits on its own, no interrogation needed (unlike classic radar, where a ground station pings the aircraft). Dependent — it depends on the aircraft's own navigation systems. The plane works out where it is from GNSS (GPS and friends), then broadcasts that answer. Surveillance — air traffic control uses it to watch traffic. Broadcast — it's one-way and unencrypted,
proposed.title: How Live Flight Tracking Actually Works: ADS-B, Explained for Developers

According to Brick Fanatics, LEGO initially described the outage as "necessary work" before confirming that the platform had suffered a security incident. In an email to users, LEGO acknowledged that "some of the information associated with your account was accessed and disclosed by an unauthorized party," including potentially usernames and IP addresses. However, the company insisted that "your password, postal address, and financial information were not disclosed." proposed.author: hammi
proposed.description: The runtime memory budget of my 1.17 MB player: keeping playback under 15 MB RAM Quick disclosure up front: I build RKMovies , an ultra-lightweight media player for Android and Windows. This is a dev diary about one number on that page: the RAM figure. Everyone asks about APK size. Nobody asks what the app does with RAM once it is running, and that is the number that actually decides whether a player survives on a 2 GB phone from 2018. So I profiled it. What I measured Setup: Android 11 phone with 2 GB RAM, playing a 1080p H.264 file with a 5.1 audio track and an SRT subtitle file. Profiler: Android Studio Memory Profiler plus dumpsys meminfo on the release build. APK is 1.17 MB; install size is a bit more because of the extracted native libs. Result: steady-state playback sits under 15 MB of app RAM. Not "15 MB at idle, 200 MB when playing". Under 15 MB while playing . Where the bytes actually go This is the part that surprised me. The video frames are not in my memory budget at all. The decoder owns the frame buffers and they live in the codec's own process memory (or shared memory with the surface), not in the app heap. If you copy frames into a Bitmap, you are doing it wrong. That alone can eat 30-80 MB on a 1080p stream. My player renders straight to a SurfaceView and never touches a pixel in app memory. What is in my heap during playback: The subtitle cue window. I parse
proposed.title: The runtime memory budget of my 1.17 MB player: keeping playback under 15 MB RAM
